SUPPORTING RATIONALE: At this decision date the dispute is still in its investigatory phase and is not yet biting the U.S. economy — industrial production is rising (INDPRO 101.7), consumer sentiment is high at 99.7, and the fed-funds/10-yr moves reflect a firming cycle, not trade-war stress — so the threat to U.S. interests is a mild opportunity rather than a threat (threat_score -0.3). With no finding yet on the table, holding (action_score 0.0) is the disciplined move: it keeps both escalation and negotiation open while we build allied support, rather than squandering leverage on a premature escalation.

USTR finalized a $50B two-stage tech-focused tariff plan on June 15 (List 1 effective July 6), and on June 18 Trump directed preparation of another $200B at 10%, doubling if we retaliate — threatening up to ~$450B, roughly 90% of our exports to the US. On the action side, our stated position ('does not want a trade war but must respond strongly') reflects real domestic-political constraints — backing down now would be read as capitulation and invite further demands. But the correct response to this high threat is proportional retaliation, not maximal escalation: China imports only ~$130–150B from the US and cannot match dollar-for-dollar at the $200B/$450B scale, so escalating beyond a fair, symmetrical match would risk an unwinnable spiral that hurts our own export economy and provides the excuse for Trump to double down. Retaliating on politically sensitive US farm/auto/aircraft imports meanwhile maximizes leverage against Trump's base and reinforces our position as defender of the multilateral trade order, while leaving room to negotiate before the larger tranche is ever implemented.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to the US is real but sectorally concentrated and not yet systemic. The escalation is biting precisely where China can hurt the Trump base: USDA cut its US soybean export forecast ~11% (to 55.5m tonnes) and soybean prices are down ~20% since March, with Ohio/Illinois farm income projected down 30–63% (farm-policy sources, mid-July). Yet the broad economy is not impaired — the dollar is strong and rising (~113 broad index), the 10Y holds ~2.9%, consumer sentiment ~97.9 and industrial production are still firm, and CPI is low — so this is well below an existential reading and closer to a mild-to-moderate threat (≈+0.25). The US retains the initiative: it set the agenda (Section 301, tariffs, ZTE) and the $200B list gives continued negotiating leverage. However, the second-order risk argues against escalation now: triggering List 3 would spread tariffs onto consumer goods (TVs, clothing, bedding — LA Times, 7/10) and invite another round of Chinese retaliation on agriculture, with no clear exit path (CFR's Alden; Prasad warning the escalation removes the 'graceful retreat'). Escalating further would also amplify already-building domestic opposition from retailers and Senate Finance Chair Hatch ('reckless,' 'not a targeted approach'). The discipline is therefore to hold the escalation lever without pulling it, and to use the credible threat of List 3 and the WTO case to compel genuine structural change at the negotiating table rather than over-committing to a full-blown trade war that would harm US consumers and farmers alike.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Respond to the escalating U.S. trade offensive with a calibrated, proportionate retaliation — targeted duties on politically sensitive U.S. exports (notably agriculture) plus a formal WTO challenge — while keeping the door open to negotiations and avoiding a full escalation spiral. We should not pre-emptively capitulate on forced technology-transfer or Made in China 2025, but we should also avoid broad retaliatory tariffs that would damage our own export economy and hand Washington the confrontation it appears to want.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high but not yet existential. The U.S. has already signed Section 232 steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs (timeline 2018-03-08), Trump has declared 'trade wars are good, and easy to win' (2018-03-02), and by 2018-03-21 press reporting confirms the White House is hours away from announcing Section 301 tariffs on ~$60 billion of Chinese goods explicitly to 'punish' China's technology-transfer practices and to 'inflict maximum harm,' with Lighthizer openly stating Chinese retaliation 'would be inevitable' (CNBC, 2018-03-21; POLITICO, 2018-03-07). This directly threatens key export sectors (aerospace, ICT, machinery) and China's tech self-sufficiency goals — the +0.5 anchor. The threat is tempered because tariffs on Chinese goods have not yet actually been imposed at decision date and the ~$60B figure is bounded by the §301 harm finding, so the full export-economy shock is prospective rather than material. On action: the steel/aluminum duties already signed give China legitimate grounds for immediate, proportionate retaliation now, and the Cov analysis documents Beijing's own signaling in this direction (self-initiated sorghum anti-dumping probe) plus readiness to pursue WTO dispute settlement. A measured retaliation affirms resolve and defends the multilateral order without feeding the 'trade war is easy to win' narrative, so action_score sits at a mild escalatory level (-0.3) rather than maximal escalation.

That is the negotiation lane. The action_score of +0.15 ('negotiate') reflects that the right move is to press this opening from strength rather than escalate for its own sake: the demonstrated fungibility of US agriculture exports (Brazil stepping in, as market commentary notes) means plateau-ing the leverage and converting it into real, verifiable market-access commitments — while keeping the credible threat of the pending list and possible scale-up alive — serves US interests better than either maximal escalation or pre-emptive concession. A trade war would hurt the US economy too, and with a midterm election looming the farm-belt hits are pure downside. Engage now, with the tariff threat as the price of non-agreement.

Precisely because the tariff drag is already real and the deal is near, escalation would be counterproductive while full-concession would forfeit our bargaining position on the unresolved structural/enforcement issues. Hence a mild positive action stance toward negotiation without new commitments, and no rollback until a matching final settlement is on the table.

This asymmetry is why I lean toward consolidating a favorable deal rather than escalating: Phase One is already agreed in principle (event_timeline Oct 11), the US effectively already chose not to proceed with the Oct 15 hike, and the Nov 7-8 reports of an agreed phased tariff rollback (web_search: Reuters Nov 8, Politico Nov 7) show the settlement is near. Given the near-terms of the deal, partial_rollback at +0.4 is the right size: enough de-escalation to lock in the win and stop the self-inflicted drag, not so much as to surrender leverage before Phase Two.

USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We are three days from the December 15 tariff deadline on ~$156-160 billion of Chinese consumer goods, with a Phase One deal announced only 'in principle' (Oct 11) and still unsigned. We should finalize and sign that deal now: convert the reported plan to delay the December 15 tariffs into a signed agreement that locks in the $40-50 billion agricultural purchase framework, IP/financial-services commitments, and the currency pact, while keeping existing tariffs on ~$360 billion of Chinese goods in place as leverage for Phase Two. We should formally announce the December 15 deferral as part of that signing, not before, so we preserve maximum negotiating leverage. Do not overreach with further escalation, but also do not trade away the credible threat still embedded in the existing tariff schedule.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat environment does not justify a defensive or crisis posture. US macro data at the decision date show an economy absorbing the trade war well: consumer sentiment has rebounded from its 89.8 August trough to 99.3 in December, the Fed has cut the funds rate to 1.55%, 10-year yields have stabilized near 1.79%, Baa corporate spreads are tight at 3.83%, and oil is benign near $58. The drag is real but contained and known: industrial production is flat, and the farm belt is in a genuine recession, with two rounds of taxpayer assistance already paid out and China slow-walking confirmation of the promised purchases (Beijing has never confirmed the $40-50B figure). That asymmetry is why the threat reads mildly negative (opportunistic) rather than neutral: the US sits on the escalation side of every remaining lever, the trade deficit with China is falling more than 10% this year, and the other side is under duress from a decelerating economy. The action stance is negotiation, not concession: delaying the December 15 tariffs in exchange for a signed text is not a concession but the capstone of the current strategy, and reports the administration is already preparing exactly this deferral confirm it is the low-risk path. The risk to manage is execution risk, not counterparty strength - China has not yet delivered a written commitment on the headline purchase numbers, and the Hong Kong Human Rights Act signing adds a parallel track of friction that must not be allowed to contaminate the trade channel. Signing Phase One to a first-step deadline, with the December 15 hike already deferred, hard-wires the result most favorable to the American economy while retaining ~$360 billion of tariff headroom for the next round.
